newsitem.title: CYPRUS: U.N. to intensify military dialogue in Cyprus.
newsitem.headline: U.N. to intensify military dialogue in Cyprus.

text.p: A United Nations-sponsored military dialogue to reduce tension between rival sides on divided Cyprus will quicken in pace to achieve a deal soon, a U.N. official said on Tuesday.
"From next week meetings will be held at an accelerated pace," said Waldemar Rokozsewski, spokesman for the United Nations force stationed on the divided island.

The U.N. proposals relate to unloading live ammunition from weapons among troops on either side of the 180 km (110 mile) long ceasefire line and unmanning sentry posts. They also impose a code of conduct for soldiers to follow.

Greek and Turkish Cypriots have been living apart since Turkey occupied northern Cyprus in 1974 in the wake of a brief Greek Cypriot coup in Nicosia backed by the military government then ruling Greece.
A force of 30,000 Turkish troops is stationed in northern Cyprus, declared a breakaway Turkish Cypriot state in 1983 recognised only by Ankara.

The U.N. believes the military measures it is proposing could help reduce tension on the island, at a peak since the deaths of four Greek Cypriots and a Turkish Cypriot last summer in separate ceasefire line incidents.
"We will have two meetings with each side each week. We believe we can achieve a deal on the entire package of measures proposed by the United Nations," said Rokoszewski.
The dialogue has been conducted by the chief of staff U.N. forces through separate meetings with the military of both sides once a week since late last year.

Earlier this month tension was again heightened on the island after disclosures the Cyprus government is buying the S-300 anti-aircraft missile system from Russia and Turkish warnings of a military strike on the island to destroy it.

Han Sung-Joo, the Secretary-general's special representative on Cyprus, arrives on the island on Wednesday for another round of contacts with both sides. U.N.-led efforts to reunite the island under a federal umbrella have so far floundered.
